claims.text: The investigated alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The alloy is evaluated in the as-cast state.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a fully solid-solution alloy.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has severe, homogeneous lattice distortion that creates high local barriers to dislocation motion.
Room-temperature deformation of HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by dislocation glide.
The room-temperature baseline has higher yield strength than the 600–1200 °C states.
The room-temperature baseline has a lower coefficient of thermal expansion than the 600–1200 °C states.
Increasing temperature thermally overcomes or reduces the effective dislocation barriers imposed by lattice distortion.
Between 600 and 1200 °C, deformation shifts from glide-dominated motion toward climb-assisted or otherwise thermally activated dislocation motion.
The elevated-temperature mechanism includes increased dynamic recovery.
The proposed mechanism transition causes a significant reduction in yield strength.
Elevated-temperature testing will produce a change in strain-hardening behavior relative to room temperature.
Elevated temperature changes the elastic moduli and elastic anisotropy of refractory high-entropy alloys.
HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit reduced shear modulus and increased elastic anisotropy at 600–1200 °C.
Enhanced atomic vibrations at elevated temperature increase the effective coefficient of thermal expansion.
The coefficient of thermal expansion of HfNbTaTiZr will be higher at 600–1200 °C than at room temperature.
Changes in mechanical and thermal responses will correlate with TEM evidence of increased dislocation climb or reorganized dislocation structures.
Short-range chemical ordering may evolve with temperature and modulate dislocation mobility.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from approximately 600 to 1200 °C under quasi-static loading.
